title: AI Industry Warns Trump’s Proposed Semiconductor Tariffs Could Stifle US Innovation
summary: The tech industry is alarmed by reports that the Trump administration may impose sweeping new semiconductor tariffs, potentially disrupting AI innovation, data center development, and consumer tech affordability. Industry groups argue the tariffs could lead to $90 billion in annual GDP losses, delay 20% of planned data center projects, and increase costs for everyday devices like smartphones and laptops. The proposed tariffs may also drive data center development overseas, contradicting the administration’s goal of boosting domestic production. While some tariff relief is under consideration, it may be tied to foreign firms investing in US chip manufacturing. The tech industry is lobbying for exemptions, particularly for data centers and AI servers, to mitigate the impact.
key_points: Trump administration may announce new semiconductor tariffs in the coming weeks or months, expanding duties to chips and downstream products like gaming consoles and servers.
Tech industry warns tariffs could cost the US $90 billion annually in GDP losses and delay or cancel 20% of data center projects through 2030.
Tariffs may increase prices for consumer devices (smartphones, laptops, vehicles) and limit technology choices, slowing AI adoption in the US.
Data center development could shift overseas due to tariffs, undermining the administration’s goal of boosting domestic production.
Industry groups estimate global semiconductor revenue will reach $1.6 trillion by 2026 due to ongoing shortages, and tariffs could further inflate chip prices.
Tariffs may disproportionately harm US chip designers like Nvidia and AMD, which rely on overseas manufacturers, while benefiting Chinese competitors.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick favors broad tariffs to prioritize reshoring the domestic supply chain, with potential duty-free allowances tied to US production pledges.
Tech industry advocates for exemptions, particularly for AI servers and data centers, and suggests lowering tariff rates to 10% to minimize economic disruption.
Critics argue domestic chip production cannot meet demand in the near term, making tariffs counterproductive for scaling AI infrastructure.
Industry groups propose nuanced tariff policies, such as exempting products with minimal semiconductor content or setting de minimis thresholds for value/weight.
